93a7c5f67472745e2a8f2a0f153e44cd66c90936.markdown:
# Coherence limits of fixed-frequency transmon qubits

## Abstract

We study what limits the energy relaxation time $T_1$ and the dephasing time $T_2$ of a fixed-frequency transmon on a sapphire substrate. Across 40 simulated devices the median $T_1$ is 110 us and the best is 310 us. Dielectric loss in the substrate-metal interface explains most of the spread, while radiative decay through the readout resonator (the Purcell effect) matters only for the strongest couplings.

## 2. Loss channels

The relaxation rate is the sum of the rates of the channels that carry energy away from the qubit:

$$\frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{T_1^{\mathrm{diel}}} + \frac{1}{T_1^{\mathrm{Purcell}}} + \frac{1}{T_1^{\mathrm{TLS}}}.$$

Dielectric loss follows the loss tangent, $1/T_1^{\mathrm{diel}} = \omega\, p_{\mathrm{surf}} \tan\delta$, where $p_{\mathrm{surf}}$ is the participation of the lossy surface. Two-level systems (TLS) in the oxide add a slowly drifting term: a qubit that crosses a TLS during a measurement loses a factor of two in $T_1$ for hours.

## 3. Dephasing

Pure dephasing adds to relaxation in the coherence time,

$$\frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{2T_1} + \frac{1}{T_\phi}.$$

For a fixed-frequency device the main source of $T_\phi$ is residual thermal photons in the readout resonator. An echo sequence removes the slow part of the noise: in our data $T_2^{\mathrm{echo}}$ is 1.6 times the Ramsey $T_2^*$. We conclude that improving the substrate surface raises $T_1$, and that filtering the readout line raises $T_2$.

112a0e0629186874853e635417ae99fcfa1a93a1.markdown:
# Surface-code memories under circuit-level noise

## Abstract

We simulate a rotated surface code of distance $d$ with depolarizing noise on every gate, idle step and measurement, decoded with minimum-weight matching. The threshold is close to 0.9% per operation. Below it, the logical error rate per round falls exponentially with the distance.

## 2. Results

Let $p$ be the physical error rate and $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ the threshold. Below threshold the logical error rate per round behaves as

$$p_L \approx A \left(\frac{p}{p_{\mathrm{th}}}\right)^{\lfloor (d+1)/2 \rfloor},$$

with $A \approx 0.1$ in our fits. At $p = 0.1\%$ the distance-5 code reaches $p_L = 3\times 10^{-5}$ and the distance-7 code reaches $4\times 10^{-6}$, so each step of two in the distance buys about a factor of eight.

## 3. Overhead

A rotated code of distance $d$ uses $d^2$ data qubits and $d^2 - 1$ measurement qubits. To keep the logical error of a computation of $10^{9}$ rounds below $10^{-3}$ at $p = 0.1\%$ we need $d \ge 13$, which is 337 physical qubits per logical qubit. A leakage-reduction step every round lowers the threshold by about a tenth of a percentage point if it is left out.

# A compact teleportation circuit with mid-circuit measurement

We give a three-qubit circuit that teleports the state of the top qubit to the bottom one using two mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled corrections.

c7f460355b1958c3e6cf45b6d3234766cd8c9d49.title: The circuit
Correctness
c7f460355b1958c3e6cf45b6d3234766cd8c9d49.markdown:
The corrected output equals $|\psi\rangle$ for every one of the four outcomes, each of which occurs with probability $1/4$:

$$|\psi_{\mathrm{out}}\rangle = X^{m_2} Z^{m_1} \, \bigl(\,\text{state after outcomes } m_1 m_2\bigr) = |\psi\rangle.$$

The circuit uses one two-qubit gate fewer than the textbook version because the Bell pair is prepared on the hardware that holds qubits 2 and 3.

0aac85046a4bd53711e94927c2741b4c1aed1658.markdown:
# Ansatz depth and barren plateaus in variational eigensolvers

## 1. Method

A variational quantum eigensolver minimizes the energy $E(\boldsymbol\theta) = \langle\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)|H|\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)\rangle$ over the parameters of a circuit. We compare a hardware-efficient ansatz with a chemistry-inspired one on a four-site Heisenberg chain, for depths from 1 to 12 layers.

## 2. Results

The hardware-efficient ansatz reaches the ground energy within $10^{-3}$ at depth 6 for 4 qubits, but at 12 qubits the variance of the gradient shrinks like $2^{-n}$ once the depth passes about $n$, the signature of a barren plateau. The chemistry-inspired ansatz keeps a gradient variance above $10^{-2}$ at every size we tried, at the price of 3 times as many two-qubit gates.

## 3. Recommendation

Start from a shallow, problem-shaped ansatz and add layers only while the energy keeps falling. Initializing the parameters near zero, so that the circuit starts close to the identity, avoided the plateau in all our runs with up to 16 qubits.

# Calibrating cross-resonance gates with echo sequences

## 1. Introduction

The cross-resonance gate drives a control qubit at the frequency of its neighbour. The effective Hamiltonian contains the wanted $ZX$ term and unwanted $IX$, $ZI$ and $ZZ$ terms. An echoed sequence with a $\pi$ pulse on the control cancels $IX$ and $ZI$ to first order.

## 2. Calibration

We calibrate the amplitude so that the $ZX$ rotation angle is $\pi/2$, $\int \Omega_{ZX}(t)\,dt = \pi/2$, and the phase of the target drive so that the residual $ZY$ term vanishes. Over 30 days the two-qubit gate error stayed between 0.6% and 1.1%, and a recalibration took 4 minutes.

# Grover search with a noisy oracle

## 1. Introduction

Grover's algorithm finds one marked item among $N$ with $O(\sqrt{N})$ oracle calls. After $k$ iterations the probability of measuring the marked item is $\sin^2\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr)$ with $\sin\theta = 1/\sqrt{N}$, which is close to 1 for $k \approx \frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N}$.

## 2. Noise in the oracle

Suppose each oracle call fails, with probability $\epsilon$, by applying a random phase. The success probability after $k$ iterations drops to roughly $P_k \approx (1-\epsilon)^k \sin^2\bigl((2k+1)\theta\bigr) + \bigl(1-(1-\epsilon)^k\bigr)/N$. For $N = 2^{10}$ and $\epsilon = 0.5\%$ the best number of iterations is 21 instead of 25, and the best success probability falls from 0.999 to 0.82.

## 3. Practical advice

Stopping early is better than running the full count when the oracle is noisy. We recommend measuring after $k^\ast = \arg\max_k P_k$ iterations and repeating the whole search a few times, which beats a longer single run once $\epsilon \sqrt{N} > 0.2$.

## 3. Dephasing

Pure dephasing adds to relaxation in the coherence time,

$$\frac{1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{2T_1} + \frac{1}{T_\phi}.$$

For a fixed-frequency device the main source of $T_\phi$ is residual thermal photons in the readout resonator. An echo sequence removes the slow part of the noise: in our data $T_2^{\mathrm{echo}}$ is 1.6 times the Ramsey $T_2^*$. We conclude that improving the substrate surface raises $T_1$, and that filtering the readout line raises $T_2$.

# Ansatz depth and barren plateaus in variational eigensolvers

## 1. Method

A variational quantum eigensolver minimizes the energy $E(\boldsymbol\theta) = \langle\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)|H|\psi(\boldsymbol\theta)\rangle$ over the parameters of a circuit. We compare a hardware-efficient ansatz with a chemistry-inspired one on a four-site Heisenberg chain, for depths from 1 to 12 layers.

contexts.name: 0aac85046a4bd537 pages 2-2
contexts.text:
## 2. Results

The hardware-efficient ansatz reaches the ground energy within $10^{-3}$ at depth 6 for 4 qubits, but at 12 qubits the variance of the gradient shrinks like $2^{-n}$ once the depth passes about $n$, the signature of a barren plateau. The chemistry-inspired ansatz keeps a gradient variance above $10^{-2}$ at every size we tried, at the price of 3 times as many two-qubit gates.

contexts.name: 0aac85046a4bd537 pages 3-3
contexts.text:
## 3. Recommendation

Start from a shallow, problem-shaped ansatz and add layers only while the energy keeps falling. Initializing the parameters near zero, so that the circuit starts close to the identity, avoided the plateau in all our runs with up to 16 qubits.
